messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amina is a thirty-eight-year-old commercial fisherman who works out of a small Gulf Coast harbor, a job that demands early mornings and long hours on the water. Eighteen months ago, her younger brother Kwame was killed in a car accident while she was driving him back to the port after a visit. A truck ran a red light and T-boned the driver’s side; Kwame died at the scene. In the months that followed, Amina could not stop replaying the moment—the screech, the impact, the terrible stillness. She would dwell on how she could have prevented it, going over every decision she made that day, certain that she should have checked the intersection before proceeding, should have seen the truck coming. This self-blame was relentless: she told herself that the accident happened because of the way she acted, that she had failed to protect her brother, and that she would never forgive herself for not doing more.

Every year on the anniversary of the crash, Amina is overwhelmed by a wave of intense fear and anger, and her body reacts with a pounding heart and trembling hands. To escape these feelings, she started staying up very late, delaying sleep so she wouldn’t have to lie in the dark replaying the crash. She also began spending money impulsively—buying clothes she didn’t need, ordering takeout she barely touched—to distract herself from the guilt. But these strategies only deepened her sense of failure. The more she spent, the more she blamed herself for being weak and irresponsible. The nights she stayed up, she would ruminate on prevention, and that rumination would bring the image of the car crash back into her mind, as vivid as the day it happened. Even without an external reminder, her own thoughts became a trigger.

Her daily life is saturated with reminders. She drives to the harbor each morning, and that commute takes her past the intersection where Kwame died. Her heart races and she feels nauseous every time she approaches it. At the dock, other fishermen sometimes talk about workplace accidents, and the word “accident” alone sends a shock through her chest, her face flushing with anger and grief. When a customer mentioned a recent car collision on the news, Amina had to walk away to keep from snapping. Her irritability has grown; she has had angry outbursts at her husband for minor things, and afterward she feels even more guilty. That guilt then drives her back to rumination or to a compulsive online shopping spree, which in turn leaves her exhausted and more irritable the next day.

Her husband finally urged her to seek help after she spent a whole paycheck on items she didn’t need and then stayed up until three in the morning replaying the crash. What frightened Amina most was that she could no longer trust herself—she felt that if she had failed to protect Kwame, she might fail again, and she could not bear that. She came to therapy hoping to stop the cycle, afraid that if she didn’t, she would lose her marriage and her livelihood, and that the guilt would never let her go.
